Verdict: The open-path descent theorem is correct. I find no fatal gap in the supplied argument. The primary Connelly–Demaine–Rote (CDR) theorem supplies the required simultaneous strict first-order expansion of all nonbar pairs, and the remaining steps produce an actual feasible diameter descent.

The important distinctions survive scrutiny:

- Straight runs are contracted before applying CDR.
- Interpolation preserves strict infinitesimal expansion across different bars.
- Reversed velocities are integrated into an exact bar-length-preserving motion.
- The exceptional diameter pairs on individual straight runs are handled by a separate, smaller perturbation.

Consequently, no unit-separated configuration of diameter D>1D>1D>1 whose complete unit-contact graph is a disjoint union of paths can be an ordinary local diameter minimum, and therefore it cannot be a global optimizer.

This is a rigorous deduction from the published CDR theorem, using the construction supplied in worker85. It is not a claim of literature novelty or a solution of Erdős Problem 99.

## 1. Precise theorem

Theorem (path-contact descent). Let P=(p1,…,pn)P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)P=(p1​,…,pn​) be a finite configuration of distinct points in R2\mathbb R^2R2, with

∣pi−pj∣≥1(i≠j),|p_i-p_j|\geq1\qquad(i\ne j),∣pi​−pj​∣≥1(i=j),

and diameter D>1D>1D>1. Suppose the complete unit-contact graph

G1(P)={{i,j}:∣pi−pj∣=1}G_1(P)=\{\{i,j\}:|p_i-p_j|=1\}G1​(P)={{i,j}:∣pi​−pj​∣=1}

is a disjoint union of finite paths and isolated vertices.

Then, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, there exists a configuration P′=(p1′,…,pn′)P'=(p'_1,\ldots,p'_n)P′=(p1′​,…,pn′​) such that

max⁡i∣pi′−pi∣<ε,∣pi′−pj′∣≥1(i≠j),diam⁡(P′)<D,\boxed{ \begin{gathered} \max_i|p'_i-p_i|<\varepsilon,\\ |p'_i-p'_j|\geq1\quad(i\ne j),\\ \operatorname{diam}(P')<D, \end{gathered}}imax​∣pi′​−pi​∣<ε,∣pi′​−pj′​∣≥1(i=j),diam(P′)<D,​​

and every original unit-contact edge still has length exactly 111.

There is no hypothesis of global optimality, density, largeness of nnn, generic position, connectedness, or stress support.

For arc-only systems, every distinct nonbar vertex pair is a strut under their framework definition. The result therefore applies simultaneously across disconnected arcs, not merely within each arc. erikdemaine.org

This is precisely the stronger infinitesimal statement needed for the proof; invoking only the continuous Carpenter's Rule theorem would leave a first-order strictness gap.

## 2. Proof and degeneracy audit

### Step A. Reduce the contact paths

Distinct unit-contact segments cannot cross at interior points. If two unit segments intersect at zzz, choose on each segment an endpoint nearest zzz. Each chosen endpoint is at distance at most 1/21/21/2 from zzz, with a strict inequality for an interior crossing. The chosen endpoints would be distinct points at distance less than 111, contradicting unit separation.

Consequently, the contact paths form disjoint simple polygonal arcs.

Compress every maximal straight chain of consecutive unit links into a single bar. Backtracking is impossible because it would repeat a point. Every resulting bar has positive integer length, and consecutive bars are noncollinear.

No other original point can lie inside a compressed bar: it would lie between consecutive original unit-spaced vertices and hence be less than one unit from one of them.

Thus the reduced system satisfies CDR's geometric hypotheses.

For each isolated point, introduce a sufficiently short auxiliary bar, disjoint from all existing arcs. Such bars exist because the original system is finite and separated. The auxiliary endpoints are discarded afterward.

Applying (1) gives velocities vav_ava​ at every reduced vertex, including the original isolated points.

px=(1−s)qA+sqB,0≤s≤1,p_x=(1-s)q_A+sq_B,\qquad 0\leq s\leq1,px​=(1−s)qA​+sqB​,0≤s≤1,

### Step D. Identify and shorten the exceptional diameters

Suppose an original diameter pair lies on one compressed bar of length mmm. Because the bar consists of mmm consecutive unit links, its endpoint distance is mmm. Thus

D≤m≤D.D\leq m\leq D.D≤m≤D.

Consequently:

m=D∈Z,m=D\in\mathbb Z,m=D∈Z,

and the diameter pair must consist of the two endpoints of the entire compressed bar.

Hence all exceptional diameter pairs are whole-run endpoint pairs, and their runs contain at least two links since D>1D>1D>1.

Fix a sufficiently small positive τ\tauτ from Step C. For each exceptional bar, rotate one constituent unit-link vector through a nonzero angle δ\deltaδ, retaining the direction of all its other links.

If uuu is the unit direction of the bar at time τ\tauτ, its new endpoint difference is

(D−1)u+Rδu.(D-1)u+R_\delta u.(D−1)u+Rδ​u.

Its squared length becomes

∣(D−1)u+Rδu∣2=(D−1)2+1+2(D−1)cos⁡δ=D2−2(D−1)(1−cos⁡δ)<D2.(6)\begin{aligned} |(D-1)u+R_\delta u|^2 &=(D-1)^2+1+2(D-1)\cos\delta\\ &=D^2-2(D-1)(1-\cos\delta)\\ &<D^2. \end{aligned} \tag{6}∣(D−1)u+Rδ​u∣2​=(D−1)2+1+2(D−1)cosδ=D2−2(D−1)(1−cosδ)<D2.​(6)

Thus every exceptional diameter strictly decreases.

Simultaneous bending is legitimate. Different compressed bars contain disjoint sets of original links, even when they share an endpoint. Altering an earlier bar may translate downstream bars, but cannot change their internal endpoint differences. The shortening calculation (6) therefore applies independently to every exceptional run.

All other pairs already have strict upper-diameter slack or retained their original subdiametral slack. Noncontacts also have strict lower-distance slack.

Because there are finitely many pairs, choose ∣δ∣>0|\delta|>0∣δ∣>0 sufficiently small that these inequalities all survive. The selected unit links remain unit length after rotation.

The final configuration is unit-separated, retains all original contacts, and has diameter strictly less than DDD.

Taking τ\tauτ and then δ\deltaδ arbitrarily small makes the final perturbation arbitrarily small.

This completes the proof. □\square□

## 3. Two unoriented contact directions

Corollary. Suppose a finite unit-separated configuration has all its unit-contact edges parallel to one of two unoriented lines, whose smaller angle is

0≤θ≤60∘.0\leq\theta\leq60^\circ.0≤θ≤60∘.

Assume its complete contact graph has no unit triangle. Then every nontrivial contact component is a monotone path. In particular, if D>1D>1D>1, the configuration is not an ordinary diameter-local minimum and cannot be a global optimizer.

Proof. Choose unit vectors u,vu,vu,v representing the two directions, with u⋅v=cos⁡θ≥1/2u\cdot v=\cos\theta\geq1/2u⋅v=cosθ≥1/2.

At any vertex, possible outgoing contact vectors belong to

{u,−u,v,−v}.\{u,-u,v,-v\}.{u,−u,v,−v}.

Two contacts in the directions u,vu,vu,v, or −u,−v-u,-v−u,−v, would place their other endpoints at distance

∣u−v∣=2sin⁡(θ/2)≤1.|u-v|=2\sin(\theta/2)\leq1.∣u−v∣=2sin(θ/2)≤1.

If this distance is less than 111, unit separation is violated. If it equals 111, the three points form a unit equilateral triangle, contrary to the hypothesis.

Thus these direction pairs are forbidden. The remaining possible pairs cannot give contact degree greater than two.

Consider an oriented component. An incoming step +u+u+u cannot be followed by −v-v−v, because the two outgoing contact rays at the intermediate vertex would be −u,−v-u,-v−u,−v. It cannot be followed by −u-u−u, because that would immediately repeat a point.

The same argument applies to all other choices. Therefore all steps along an oriented component belong either to

{u,v}or to{−u,−v}.\{u,v\}\quad\text{or to}\quad\{-u,-v\}.{u,v}or to{−u,−v}.

The projection onto u+vu+vu+v is strictly monotone along every nontrivial component. No component can be a cycle.

Thus all components are monotone paths or isolates, and the theorem applies. □\square□

In fact, triangle-freeness is redundant when the complete contact graph uses at most two unoriented directions: an equilateral triangle requires three distinct edge directions.

Therefore the exclusion applies to every local minimum with D>1D>1D>1 whose entire contact graph uses at most two directions separated by at most 60∘60^\circ60∘.

## 4. Scope, references, and remaining blocker

The proved obstruction is exact and finite. Every diameter-local minimum with D>1D>1D>1 must have a contact graph containing either a cycle or a vertex of degree at least three.

It does not exclude arbitrary triangle-free graphs. Vertices of degree three and cycles of length four or greater remain admissible. CDR's path theorem cannot automatically be applied to branched contact frameworks.

Nor does this result establish a density gap, a large stressed component, or a transition from arbitrary triangle-free global optimizers to two-direction contact graphs.

## Result: the proposed max-degree-two theorem admits a proof

The second-order obstruction from straight diameter runs can be eliminated simultaneously. The essential observation is that the squared-distance shortening of a straight run depends only on its first-order changes of link angles, not on the second-order corrections needed to close a cycle.

This yields the proposed statement for every finite configuration, without a largeness assumption.

The argument below combines Connelly–Demaine–Rote's (CDR) published infinitesimal theorem with the angle-coordinate and second-order extension developed from the supplied approach. I make no claim that this consequence is new to the literature or has been independently peer-reviewed.

### Theorem (max-degree-two contact obstruction)

Let P={p1,…,pn}⊂R2P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\subset\mathbb R^2P={p1​,…,pn​}⊂R2 be distinct points satisfying

∣pi−pj∣≥1(i≠j).|p_i-p_j|\geq1\qquad(i\ne j).∣pi​−pj​∣≥1(i=j).

Let D=diam⁡(P)>1D=\operatorname{diam}(P)>1D=diam(P)>1, and let G(P)G(P)G(P) be its complete unit-contact graph, containing exactly the pairs at distance 111.

Assume:

1. Every vertex of G(P)G(P)G(P) has degree at most two.
2. PPP is an ordinary local minimum of diameter among all sufficiently nearby configurations satisfying the same unit-separation inequalities.

Then G(P)G(P)G(P) contains a simple convex cycle CCC, every edge of which has length 111, such that

diam⁡(V(C))=D.\boxed{\operatorname{diam}(V(C))=D.}diam(V(C))=D.​

Here convex allows consecutive collinear edges. Local minimality is not restricted to a prescribed contact graph.

### Proof

1. Contact components form an embedded arc-and-cycle set.

Because all pairwise distances are at least 111, two distinct unit segments cannot cross in their relative interiors.

Indeed, if they crossed at xxx, choose from each segment an endpoint at distance at most 1/21/21/2 from xxx. These two endpoints would have mutual distance strictly less than 111. Overlapping segments or vertices lying inside nonincident unit segments are excluded similarly.

Thus the components of G(P)G(P)G(P) are noncrossing polygonal paths, simple polygonal cycles, and isolated vertices.

Within a collinear contact path, successive edges must point in the same traversal direction: reversal would repeat a vertex.

2. Obtain a weak contraction from CDR.

For a velocity assignment v=(vi)v=(v_i)v=(vi​), write

Qij(v)=(pj−pi)⋅(vj−vi).Q_{ij}(v)=(p_j-p_i)\cdot(v_j-v_i).Qij​(v)=(pj​−pi​)⋅(vj​−vi​).

Its sign is the sign of the first derivative of the corresponding squared distance.

CDR, §2.2–3, Theorem 3, constructs a strict infinitesimal expansive motion for a reduced arc-and-cycle framework. Their reductions coalesce straight subarcs, rigidify convex cycles, and remove components nested inside convex cycles. erikdemaine.org erikdemaine.org

Applying that theorem and reversing velocities yields an infinitesimal contact-preserving motion v0v^0v0 satisfying

Qij(v0)≤0Q_{ij}(v^0)\leq0Qij​(v0)≤0

for every pair, with strict inequality unless the two points:

- belong to one straight subarc of contact edges; or
- lie on or inside a common convex contact cycle.

Here is why these strict inequalities extend to all the original vertices, rather than just the reduced framework.

On a coalesced straight bar ABABAB, restore an intermediate vertex X=(1−s)A+sBX=(1-s)A+sBX=(1−s)A+sB with interpolated velocity vX=(1−s)vA+svBv_X=(1-s)v_A+sv_BvX​=(1−s)vA​+svB​. Then

QXY=(1−s)QAY+sQBYQ_{XY}=(1-s)Q_{AY}+sQ_{BY}QXY​=(1−s)QAY​+sQBY​

because QAB=0Q_{AB}=0QAB​=0. Applying the identity twice handles vertices on two reduced bars.

For a component nested inside a convex cycle, CDR carries it by the same infinitesimal rigid motion as that cycle. Expressing an interior point as a convex combination of boundary vertices gives the corresponding identity for its distance from an exterior vertex. All internal boundary-distance derivatives vanish, while exterior derivatives are strictly signed. This is the infinitesimal version of CDR's Lemma 2. erikdemaine.org

Consequently, strict contraction holds for every pair outside those two exceptional classes.

Suppose now, toward contradiction, that no convex contact cycle has diameter DDD.

Every convex contact cycle then has diameter strictly less than DDD. Moreover, all vertices of contact components nested inside it lie in its convex hull.

Hence no actual diameter pair can have both endpoints on or inside one convex contact cycle.

It follows that every diameter pair (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) either satisfies

Qij(v0)<0,Q_{ij}(v^0)<0,Qij​(v0)<0,

or lies on a straight contact subarc.

We call the latter pairs flat diameter pairs.

3. Every flat diameter pair can be bent infinitesimally.

Suppose a flat diameter pair is joined by mmm consecutive unit links, all pointing along the same unit vector uuu. Necessarily

Parametrize contact-link vectors by their angles:

There are finitely many flat diameter pairs. For each one, the tangent flex space contains a vector whose angular rates on that subarc are not all equal.

The vectors whose rates are all equal on a specified subarc form a proper linear subspace.

A finite union of proper linear subspaces cannot exhaust a real vector space. Therefore there exists one infinitesimal contact-preserving flex www whose angular rates are nonconstant on every flat diameter subarc simultaneously.

We have therefore found a single infinitesimal contact-preserving motion that strictly contracts every nonflat diameter pair to first order and bends every flat diameter subarc nonuniformly.

For a flat diameter subarc containing m≥2m\geq2m≥2 unit links, let their angular rates under vvv be a1,…,ama_1,\ldots,a_ma1​,…,am​.

and

∣pj(t)−pi(t)∣<D|p_j(t)-p_i(t)|<D∣pj​(t)−pi​(t)∣<D

for all sufficiently small t>0t>0t>0.

Every nonflat diameter pair also shortens, already to first order.

Since there are finitely many pairs, all initially subdiametral pairs remain strictly below DDD for sufficiently small ttt.

Thus

diam⁡(P(t))<D,\operatorname{diam}(P(t))<D,diam(P(t))<D,

The contradiction proves the theorem. □\square□

### Consequences and limitations

The proof handles the potential difficulties in the proposed extension:

- Simultaneous flat runs: a generic tangent flex bends them all; their quadratic shortening cannot be canceled by closure corrections.
- Cycle closure: the unit-edge angle constraint has rank two for every simple cycle, including one with collinear consecutive edges.
- Nested components: CDR's convex-cycle reduction supplies the necessary first-order signs; nested components cannot contain a diameter pair internally unless the containing cycle already spans DDD.
- Small diameters: when 1<D<21<D<21<D<2, no flat diameter subarc exists, so the first-order argument alone suffices.

This does not prove Erdős Problem 99. The hypothesis concerns the complete unit-contact graph of a particular local minimizer. There is no established argument here forcing the contact graph of every sufficiently large global optimizer, or even a suitably chosen global optimizer, to have maximum degree two.

In particular, the theorem makes no claim that a degree-three contact can be eliminated without losing global optimality. It also does not rule out triangle-free local minima whose convex unit cycles themselves span the diameter.

The result is an exact finite-configuration obstruction, not a density-gap statement.

## 6. Adversarial relevance test: does the deficit force a unit triangle?

No. This is the decisive limitation.

The result proves a uniform convex-hull area/perimeter defect. It does not establish the existence of three original points whose pairwise distances all equal exactly 111.

There are several reasons not to make that inference.

### 6.1 Wegner equality is not the diameter-minimization objective

Wegner's theorem concerns the area of the convex hull of congruent disks. Its equality cases are special finite densest packings, called Wegner packings.

For those packings, the centre hull has the specified quantized perimeter. After our scaling, that perimeter is sns_nsn​.

Our result instead establishes

P(X)≤23π(n−1)<sn.P(X)\le\sqrt{2\sqrt3\pi(n-1)}<s_n.P(X)≤23​π(n−1)​<sn​.

It excludes Wegner equality for global diameter minimizers at n≥301n\ge301n≥301.

But it does not say that every non-Wegner packing is triangle-free, or that every non-Wegner packing contains a unit triangle.

Indeed, a configuration can contain several unit equilateral triangles and still have strict Wegner inequality.

### 6. Audit of the Voronoi, Gabriel and Delaunay assumptions

There are several distinctions that matter.

| Geometric object | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original unit contact | Exact distance one | An equilateral triangle |
| Gabriel edge | Empty diametral disk | Unit edge length |
| Delaunay edge | Empty-circle adjacency | Unit edge length |
| Voronoi facet neighbor | A genuine shared Voronoi boundary | Unit edge length |
| Six near-unit Voronoi neighbors | Nearhexagonal local geometry | Six exact contacts |
| Six exact unit neighbors | Exact unit equilateral triangle | Nothing further is needed |

An original unit contact is indeed a Gabriel edge: its closed diametral disk cannot contain another original site, since every point in that disk other than its endpoints would be at distance less than one from both endpoints.

Gabriel edges are therefore contained in the Delaunay graph.

The converse is not true. The oblique lattice above gives actual Voronoi neighbors at distances strictly greater than one.

There is also a degeneracy issue. A Delaunay triangulation may insert arbitrary diagonals into a cocircular Delaunay face. Such diagonals need not correspond to positive-length shared Voronoi facets.

Consequently, the W117 six-neighbor theorem must establish six distinct original facet-neighbors, not merely six incidences in an arbitrarily chosen Delaunay triangulation.

### 5.1 W124: stress support, not full active rigidity

Dalton's stress-union result, independently accepted by Aquinas, concerns the union E∗E_*E∗​ of edges receiving positive support under at least one normalized nonnegative equilibrium stress.

rank⁡R(E∗)≤2n−4.\boxed{\operatorname{rank}R(E_*)\leq2n-4.}rankR(E∗​)≤2n−4.​

Aquinas's stronger generic-stratum statement is also carefully scoped:

If a fixed nnn has infinitely many congruence classes of exact global minimizers, one can select a suitable smooth semialgebraic stratum on which the active contact and diameter-pair sets are locally constant. At an appropriate optimizer on that stratum,

rank⁡R(C∪H)≤2n−4,\operatorname{rank}R(C\cup H)\leq2n-4,rankR(C∪H)≤2n−4,

The n=8n=8n=8 apex example is an important adversarial test:

- its full active bar graph has rank 13=2(8)−313=2(8)-313=2(8)−3;

Let Mn\mathcal M_nMn​ denote the class of all unrestricted exact global diameter minimizers with nnn distinct original sites and mutual distances at least one.

The positive assertion is

> Edge Bounds and Degeneracy of Triangle-Free Penny Graphs and Squaregraphs, Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications 22(3), 2018, pp. 483–499.

For a triangle-free penny graph GGG on nnn vertices, Eppstein proves

∣E(G)∣≤min⁡{2n−Ω(n),2n−DG−2},\boxed{ |E(G)|\le \min\{2n-\Omega(\sqrt n),\,2n-D_G-2\}, }∣E(G)∣≤min{2n−Ω(n​),2n−DG​−2},​

where DGD_GDG​ is the graph diameter. He also proves that every triangle-free penny graph is 2-degenerate. Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications+1

This is stronger than the elementary triangle-free planar bound m≤2n−4m\le 2n-4m≤2n−4, but its most important feature for Erdős #99 is the boundary deficit: a large triangle-free penny graph cannot have nearly 2n2n2n contacts.

The unresolved step is on the other side of the comparison: one would need a sufficiently strong lower bound on the number of active unit contacts in every exact unrestricted global diameter optimizer. A local rigidity count, an assumed generic configuration, or a lower bound for a selected optimizer is not enough.

The analysis below separates what follows rigorously from planar graph theory, what follows from Eppstein's geometric theorem, and what would still be needed to prove the original universal statement.

The proof of Theorem 1 contains an especially useful geometric observation:

The argument uses turning angles along the outer boundary. At a boundary vertex of degree at least three, the relevant signed turning contribution is nonpositive. However, it does not say that all low-degree vertices must be original convex-hull vertices. Eppstein explicitly notes that the convex-hull vertices can all have degree three in a triangle-free penny graph. Thus an argument assigning all the degeneracy deficit to the convex hull would be invalid.

### 4.1 What the dual interpretation says

The dual graph of the triangulation has one vertex for each triangular face.

Every interior noncontact edge corresponds to an edge joining two dual vertices. Every noncontact hull edge corresponds to a boundary half-edge.

Because each triangle must have at least one noncontact edge, these dual edges and boundary half-edges form an edge cover of the triangular faces.

The equality case

σ=q∂=0\sigma=q_{\partial}=0σ=q∂​=0

is particularly informative:

1. Every triangle has exactly one noncontact edge.
2. Every noncontact edge is interior.
3. Every noncontact edge pairs two triangular faces.
4. Each paired pair of triangles forms a rhombus with four unit sides.

Thus the triangulation decomposes into unit rhombi.

Matched dual faces

Two triangles paired across one long diagonal.

Rhombus geometry

Four unit sides; both diagonals exceed one in the triangle-free case.

If the rhombus angle is θ\thetaθ, its diagonal lengths are

2sin⁡(θ/2),2cos⁡(θ/2).2\sin(\theta/2),\qquad 2\cos(\theta/2).2sin(θ/2),2cos(θ/2).

π3<θ<2π3.\frac{\pi}{3}<\theta<\frac{2\pi}{3}.3π​<θ<32π​.

Its area is

Arhombus=sin⁡θ>32.A_{\mathrm{rhombus}}=\sin\theta>\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.Arhombus​=sinθ>23​​.

But the excess can be arbitrarily small: take θ\thetaθ arbitrarily close to 60∘60^\circ60∘.

This last fact is a serious obstruction to a simple area-based proof. Triangle-freeness does not produce a uniform positive excess over the optimal triangular-lattice cell area.

## 8. Discharging assessment and remaining proof gaps

The investigation gives four distinct conclusions.

A. The planar upper-bound machinery is strong enough to be useful.

Eppstein's 2n−1.6495n+O(1)2n-1.6495\sqrt n+O(1)2n−1.6495n​+O(1) bound is substantially sharper than elementary Euler counting. His four-low-degree-vertices lemma provides additional geometric information that could be combined with diameter constraints.

B. Disconnectedness is not a technical nuisance that can be ignored.

The exact n=8n=8n=8 global optimizer has contact graph C7⊔K1C_7\sqcup K_1C7​⊔K1​. The component correction in (2) and the dual defect terms in (3) correctly account for this configuration.

C. The dual matching reduction identifies a potentially useful structural regime.

A triangle-free optimizer with few dual defects would have a contact graph close to a rhombus quadrangulation. Such a structure might be attacked through geometric deformation, boundary curvature, or global diameter comparisons.

But the square-grid and oblique-lattice examples show that the dual matching condition itself does not force a unit triangle.

### 5.2 Triangular hulls cannot simply be ignored

- One active edge: at least one endpoint must move.
- Two active edges: a common endpoint may cover both.
- Three active edges: at least two hull vertices must move.

There is no general guarantee that a low-degree contact vertex is one of the required diameter endpoints.

Points lying in the relative interior of a hull side are also important. They may carry unit contacts and constrain a shear, while not themselves belonging to the diameter graph.

## 6. What would be needed to turn this into a large-nnn theorem?

The exact n=8n=8n=8 example and the path-folding countertest identify two separate gaps.

Gap A — Boundary selection.

One would need to show that triangle-free global minimizers with sufficiently many points possess a boundary subset covering every active diameter pair and admitting a jointly feasible motion.

Eppstein's degeneracy theorem does not provide this.

Gap B — Breaking mixed stresses.

Even if such a subset exists, one must show that its contact constraints cannot support a mixed equilibrium blocking simultaneous diameter contraction.

The heptagon stress shows that this assertion is false without a sufficiently-large-nnn qualification.

More importantly, the existence of a first-order stress is not itself the end of the problem. A proposed proof must either:

1. rule out the relevant stress configurations for all sufficiently large triangle-free global minimizers; or
2. establish a genuinely nonlinear feasible replacement that defeats the stress.

A path of unit contacts is insufficient, and a contact-graph edge bound is insufficient.

The exact global comparison must concern the entire original configuration and every active diameter pair.

## 5. The contact graph obstruction

The distinction between the Voronoi graph and the unit-contact graph is essential.

- The Voronoi/Delaunay adjacency graph records which sites define cell boundaries.
- The unit-contact graph records only pairs at distance exactly one.

The six neighbors of a nearregular cell belong to the first graph. They need not belong to the second.

David Eppstein's published result is particularly relevant here.

For triangle-free penny graphs, Eppstein proves:

1. Degeneracy at most two.
2. At most 2n−DG−22n-D_G-22n−DG​−2 edges for a connected graph of graph diameter DGD_GDG​.
3. In particular, at most 2n−Ω(n)2n-\Omega(\sqrt n)2n−Ω(n​) edges.

Here a penny graph is the contact graph of nonoverlapping equal disks, so its edges represent exact tangencies, not approximate contacts. jgaa.info+1

There is also a useful Voronoi-area lemma in the same paper: for a vertex not on the outer face of a triangle-free penny-graph representation, its Voronoi cell has area at least that of a regular hexagon circumscribed around the disk. jgaa.info

This is consistent with the area method, but it does not activate exact contacts.

A triangle-free contact graph can be sparse while its underlying point configuration has many nearunit Voronoi neighbors. Eppstein's degeneracy result actually warns against assuming that a nearly triangular Voronoi adjacency graph must be a triangular contact graph.

The precise missing bridge is therefore not another planar edge count. It is a theorem converting small positive Voronoi support slacks into exact active contact constraints under global diameter extremality.

The existing estimates do not provide that conversion.

## 8. Wegner and Oler: what equality would give

There is a potentially attractive but invalid shortcut worth separating from the argument above.

The Thue–Groemer inequality has an exact equality characterization. In the nondegenerate case, equality requires a triangulation of the center hull into regular triangles of side length two in the unit-disc normalization.

After rescaling to minimum point separation one, these become unit equilateral triangles.

Likewise, Böröczky and Ruzsa's account of Wegner's inequality identifies equality for particular densest finite disk packings. users.renyi.hu

However, three different optimization problems must not be confused:

1. Minimizing the diameter of the centers.
2. Minimizing the area of the convex hull of the centers.
3. Minimizing the area of the convex hull of the disks.

The equality characterizations for the latter two do not characterize every minimizer of the first.

Indeed, Böröczky and Ruzsa explicitly formulate as a conjecture that every densest packing of nnn unit discs is a Groemer packing. Their paper establishes Wegner's inequality and its equality characterization, not that universal structural conjecture.

Thus the following inference is unavailable:

D(X)=Dn⟹equality in Oler or Wegner⟹unit equilateral triangles.D(X)=D_n \Longrightarrow \text{equality in Oler or Wegner} \Longrightarrow \text{unit equilateral triangles}.D(X)=Dn​⟹equality in Oler or Wegner⟹unit equilateral triangles.

What is available is approximate equality at the leading density scale. The O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​) boundary allowance is precisely large enough to accommodate small positive cell-area defects without exact equality.

This is consistent with the near-contact obstruction in Section 4.

## 9. Audit of possible infinite-family constructions

The following is my classification of the candidate mechanisms.

| Proposed mechanism | What it establishes | What remains missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regular polygons | Exact finite counterexamples | Arbitrarily large exact globality |
| Regular heptagon with free center | Continuum of n=8n=8n=8 exact optimizers | An additional feasible site |
| Delete a free site | A feasible smaller configuration | Its unrestricted optimality |
| Add a separated interior point | Exact extension if it fits within the old diameter | Infinitely many such extensions |
| Uniform scaling | A normalized packing | Exact equality with DnD_nDn​ |
| Generic perturbation | Triangle-free near-optimizers | Attainment of the infimum |
| Square-grid or oblique-lattice patches | Feasible packings and contact graphs | Exact unrestricted lower bounds |
| Triangular-lattice patches | Asymptotically efficient packings | Exact finite global optimality and control of all original contacts |
| Numerical nine-point constructions | Upper bounds | A global certificate |
| Triangle-free planar contact graphs | Sparse contact graphs | A matching global-optimality construction |

### The most significant failure modes

A. Taking a subset of an optimizer

The subset's diameter may be larger than the new cardinality's optimal diameter. The n=8n=8n=8 to n=7n=7n=7 example demonstrates this exactly.

B. Taking a superset of an optimizer

A new point must satisfy both separation and diameter constraints simultaneously. Free movement of an existing site does not imply this.

C. Perturbing all unit contacts

Perturbation destroys exact contacts but generally changes the diameter. Renormalization restores minimum separation, not global optimality.

D. Proving an extremal result in a restricted family

An optimal regular polygon, rhombus, lattice patch or symmetric packing need not be an unrestricted optimizer. The unrestricted competitor space is essential.

E. Using asymptotic density as an exact certificate

An o(1)o(1)o(1) error in normalized diameter can still be strictly positive for every finite nnn. The target is exact equality at each cardinality, not convergence.

## 11. Final assessment: the smallest missing implication

The different routes examined here lead to the same unresolved obstruction.

Convex packing dual: Oler's inequality provides the exact global density bound, but triangle-free packings can approach its equality value arbitrarily closely.

Translative lattice rigidity: A lattice achieves optimal determinant only at the triangular lattice, but oblique lattices approach that determinant while remaining exactly triangle-free.

Periodic rigidity: There are strong theorems for restricted collectively jammed torus packings, but no established transfer from finite diameter optimization to periodic jamming.

Saturated insertion: Exact globality forbids replacement of a diameter-graph vertex cover, but there is no proven insertion-capacity estimate forcing such a replacement in the triangle-free case.

Contact-graph topology: Triangle-free penny graphs are sparse and have low-degree vertices, but low-degree vertices can be locally movable or pinned by diameter constraints. Neither alternative forces a unit triangle.

The smallest missing rigorous implication is therefore:

X is an exact global diameter minimizer,n sufficiently large,G1(X) contains no triangle⟹there exists a feasible strict diameter descent.\boxed{ \begin{gathered} X\text{ is an exact global diameter minimizer},\\ n\text{ sufficiently large},\\ G_1(X)\text{ contains no triangle} \\[2mm] \Longrightarrow\\[2mm] \text{there exists a feasible strict diameter descent.} \end{gathered} }X is an exact global diameter minimizer,n sufficiently large,G1​(X) contains no triangle⟹there exists a feasible strict diameter descent.​​

The oblique-lattice constructions show that this implication cannot follow merely from asymptotic density, near-regular geometry, near-optimal diameter, saturation, or small packing slackness. It must exploit something genuinely specific to exact global diameter minimality and the finite boundary.

Conversely, a disproof still requires infinitely many nnn for which an explicit triangle-free configuration is proved to attain the unrestricted exact DnD_nDn​. None of the constructions here meets that standard.

At any site, its unit-contact neighbors lie on the unit circle. If two such neighbors subtend angle θ\thetaθ, their mutual distance is

2sin⁡(θ/2)≥1.2\sin(\theta/2)\geq1.2sin(θ/2)≥1.

Thus their angular separation is at least 60∘60^\circ60∘. Equality creates an original unit equilateral triangle, so in a triangle-free configuration every such separation is strictly greater than 60∘60^\circ60∘.

It follows that

deg⁡E(i)≤5.(16)\boxed{\deg_{\mathcal E}(i)\leq5.} \tag{16}degE​(i)≤5.​(16)

There is a further constraint on the stress support:

- A vertex in S∖BS\setminus BS∖B cannot have positive contact degree one.
- If it has degree exactly two, its two unit-contact vectors must be opposite, with equal stress weights.

Thus every such degree-two interior stress vertex lies on a straight unit-contact path.

Combining (14)–(16), a triangle-free exact optimizer must have a positive contact-stress graph with:

- at most h/2h/2h/2 connected components;
- at least two diameter-stressed hull anchors per component;
- no degree-one vertices away from the diameter-stressed set;
- maximum contact degree five;
- straight-through geometry at every degree-two non-diameter-stressed vertex.

These are exact conditions, not near-unit approximations.

## 6. A rigorous local sufficiency theorem

The preceding distinction can be made precise.

### Proposition 6.1 — Strict stress plus infinitesimal rigidity implies local optimality

Suppose a feasible configuration XXX, of diameter D>1D>1D>1, has the following properties:

1. There are KKT weights satisfying equilibrium (1)–(2).
2. Every active constraint has strictly positive multiplier: \[ \alpha_e>0\quad(e\in\mathcal E),\qquad \beta_f>0\quad(f\in\mathcal F). \]
3. The framework formed by all active edges E∪F\mathcal E\cup\mathcal FE∪F, on their incident vertices, is infinitesimally rigid in the plane.

Then XXX is a local minimum of diameter among unit-separated configurations, modulo rigid motions of the active framework.

Points not incident to any active constraint can remain locally free.

Proof.

Suppose, to the contrary, there were feasible configurations Y(k)→XY^{(k)}\to XY(k)→X with diameters Rk<DR_k<DRk​<D.

Align the active framework by rigid motions and normalize its nonzero displacement by its norm. Passing to a subsequence gives a nonzero limiting velocity vvv, chosen orthogonal to infinitesimal rigid motions.

For every contact edge, the separation inequality implies

re⋅(vi−vj)≥0.r_e\cdot(v_i-v_j)\geq0.re​⋅(vi​−vj​)≥0.

For every diameter edge, the strict decrease in diameter implies

rf⋅(vi−vj)≤0.r_f\cdot(v_i-v_j)\leq0.rf​⋅(vi​−vj​)≤0.

By equilibrium,

∑fβfrf⋅(vi−vj)=∑eαere⋅(vi−vj).\sum_f\beta_f r_f\cdot(v_i-v_j) = \sum_e\alpha_e r_e\cdot(v_i-v_j).f∑​βf​rf​⋅(vi​−vj​)=e∑​αe​re​⋅(vi​−vj​).

The left side is nonpositive and the right side nonnegative. They must both vanish.

Since all multipliers are strictly positive, every active edge has zero first-order length change:

rij⋅(vi−vj)=0({i,j}∈E∪F).r_{ij}\cdot(v_i-v_j)=0 \qquad (\{i,j\}\in\mathcal E\cup\mathcal F).rij​⋅(vi​−vj​)=0({i,j}∈E∪F).

Infinitesimal rigidity implies that vvv is a rigid motion. But the alignment removed all such motions, contradicting its nonzero normalization.

Therefore no sequence of smaller-diameter configurations can converge to XXX. □\square□

This proposition is a useful sufficient local criterion. It is not a global optimality theorem.

The following two exact examples illustrate both its usefulness and its limitation.

### 8.4 What this countertest establishes

The square and n=8n=8n=8 examples jointly demonstrate:

- Strictly positive equilibrium stresses do not imply unit triangles.
- The active diameter graph can be a set of long crossing chords.
- The active framework can be infinitesimally rigid and still have triangle-free contact graphs.
- An exact global optimizer can have original sites with every pairwise distance strictly between one and the diameter.
- The KKT stress matrix need not be PSD; in fact its trace is negative.

These examples do not disprove the eventual Erdős conjecture. They show why neither stress equilibrium nor active-framework rigidity is sufficient.

A triangle-free unit rhombus can have angle

## 10. The specific global inequality still missing

The results above suggest a fairly precise formulation of what a successful stress-based proof would need.

Let XXX be an exact optimizer with KKT weights (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β). Its positive diameter stress is supported on antipodal exposed hull vertices. Its positive contact stress consists of components with at least two such anchors.

Every hypothetical better planar packing Y=X+VY=X+VY=X+V must satisfy

Q(V)<0,Q(V)<0,Q(V)<0,

where

Q(V)=∑f∈Fβf∣vi−vj∣2−∑e∈Eαe∣vi−vj∣2.Q(V)= \sum_{f\in\mathcal F}\beta_f|v_i-v_j|^2 - \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\alpha_e|v_i-v_j|^2.Q(V)=f∈F∑​βf​∣vi​−vj​∣2−e∈E∑​αe​∣vi​−vj​∣2.

A successful exclusion argument could proceed in either of two ways.

Route A — planar stress inequality.

Establish a lower bound on Q(V)Q(V)Q(V) for all feasible planar displacements, using:

- the normal cones at the diameter-stressed hull vertices;
- the componentwise force-balance condition;
- the triangle-free angular separation;
- the actual planar rank-two geometry;
- the diameter constraints on all original pairs, not merely the active ones.

The target would be a contradiction to Q(V)<0Q(V)<0Q(V)<0.

Route B — componentwise boundary pinning.

Show that the positive contact-stress components cannot collectively accommodate the required diameter forces unless at least one component contains an original unit triangle.

The component anchoring lemma gives a starting point: each component must have at least two diameter-stressed hull anchors, and its resultant directions must balance.

But neither the antipodal-anchor condition nor the stress edge-count inequality presently implies a unit triangle.

In particular, a two-anchor component can have opposite resultants without its anchors being separated by DDD. This prevents a direct identification of contact paths with actual diameter paths.

### What I cannot justify

I cannot prove any of the following:

1. That every positive-stress component must contain a unit triangle.
2. That a sufficiently large triangle-free contact graph cannot satisfy the hull-cone equilibrium equations.
3. That the diameter-stressed hull vertices must force a particular triangulation of the interior.
4. That the Oler slack in a triangle-free exact optimizer has a lower bound exceeding the available boundary slack.
5. That a KKT stress satisfying the necessary equations must be globally sufficient.

The last point is especially important: the square and the n=8n=8n=8 optimizer satisfy very strong local conditions, but those conditions do not distinguish exact global optimality from a potentially nonglobal local minimum.

## 8. The remaining global surgery problem

The preceding calculations give a relatively sharp formulation of what would need to be proved.

Suppose X∈MnX\in\mathcal M_nX∈Mn​ is triangle-free.

A successful surgery must simultaneously:

1. Move at least one endpoint of every diametral pair.
2. Preserve every unit-contact constraint, including contacts crossing the replacement boundary.
3. Keep every noncontact pair at distance at least one.
4. Strictly shorten every original diametral pair, or otherwise ensure that the new maximum distance is strictly below DnD_nDn​.
5. Use exactly nnn original sites in the replacement configuration.

The first condition says that the surgery support must be a vertex cover of the diameter graph.

The second and third conditions are encoded by the contact inequalities in Lemma 6.

The fourth is encoded by its strict diameter inequalities.

The fifth prevents the usual escape into a lower-cardinality packing problem.

The two-direction lattice calculation supplies a useful conditional theorem: if the active diameter differences all have one strict coordinate-product sign, and the cross-boundary contact derivatives are compatible, a global shear gives a rigorous contradiction.

The equal-diagonal square example shows that the active diameter graph can contain both signs, blocking this argument.

The fixed-collar theorem shows that even a bulk of n−O(n)n-O(\sqrt n)n−O(n​) nearhexagonal sites can be locally immovable when an O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​) boundary is held fixed.

These are genuine obstructions, not merely technical inconveniences.

### 8.1 The boundary stress problem

The most promising remaining formulation is:

Boundary-pinning problem. Can an exact global triangle-free configuration support a nonnegative equilibrium stress that balances all diameter-active constraints while freezing an asymptotically full nearhexagonal contact patch?

A proof of impossibility would be valuable. It would turn the structural nearhexagonal information into an all-global theorem.

A construction of such a stress is not itself a counterexample. It must be realized by an exact globally optimal configuration, with the correct unrestricted diameter.

Its abstract establishes a stress framework for every minimizer, an adapted frozen-contact support, and a reduction to O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​)-scale boundary pinning. My fixed-collar calculation is an explicit elementary model of how boundary pinning can work. It does not prove that the required stress can occur in an exact global minimizer, nor does it eliminate more general train-track or nonlattice deformations.
